young.html: Fyodor Dostoevsky (say dos-tuh-YEF-skee) was a Russian novelist. As a young man he was arrested for joining a group that discussed forbidden ideas, sentenced to death, and pardoned at the very last moment. He spent years in a prison camp in Siberia. Afterward he wrote some of the deepest novels ever written about right and wrong, faith and doubt.

The Brothers Karamazov is about three very different brothers. Dmitri is wild and passionate. Ivan is brilliant and full of questions. Alyosha, the youngest, is gentle and kind, and wants to help everyone. Their father is a selfish man who never took care of them, and the story is partly a mystery about what happened to him.

young.html: Alyosha's teacher, a wise old monk named Father Zosima, teaches that we are all responsible for each other and should love the whole world, "every grain of sand in it." At the end, Alyosha asks a group of schoolboys to always remember the good they felt when they were kind together.

For parents: this is a novel for older teens and adults. Its mystery is a murder, and some chapters discuss suffering, including Ivan's arguments, which the lesson summarizes without detail. Younger readers can enjoy the boys' chapters about Ilyusha (Book X) and the Epilogue.

Remember a kindness. Alyosha tells the boys that one good memory can help a person all their life. Write or draw a memory of a time someone was kind to you, or you to someone. Keep it somewhere you will see it.

full.html: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was arrested in 1849 for taking part in a radical discussion circle, faced a firing squad, and was reprieved at the last moment; he served four years at hard labor in Siberia, reading only the New Testament. He returned a believing Orthodox Christian and the author of Crime and Punishment and other great novels. The Brothers Karamazov, his last, appeared as a magazine serial in 1879–80; he died a few months later. Constance Garnett's translation (1912) introduced it to many English readers.

full.name: gb-karamazov-family
full.cap: Our map of the Karamazovs and those around them.

full.html: Fyodor Karamazov, a greedy, mocking landowner, quarrels with his eldest son Dmitri over an inheritance and a woman, Grushenka. When Fyodor is found murdered, Dmitri is arrested. The middle brother Ivan, an intellectual, has been arguing that without God and immortality "everything is lawful" (in Garnett's words), and the servant Smerdyakov, rumored to be another son, has been listening. Alyosha, the youngest, a novice at the local monastery, tries to love them all.
In the book's most famous chapters, Ivan tells Alyosha why he cannot accept God's world: he cannot accept a world in which innocent children suffer, even if it all comes right in the end.

full.text:
"It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return Him the ticket."

"That's rebellion," murmured Alyosha, looking down.
full.author: Dostoevsky
full.work: The Brothers Karamazov, Book V, Chapter IV, "Rebellion"

full.html: Then Ivan tells his prose poem "The Grand Inquisitor": Christ returns to 16th-century Spain, and an aged cardinal has him arrested. People cannot bear the freedom you gave them, the Inquisitor says; we have given them bread, miracles and authority instead. Christ says nothing and, at the end, kisses the old man. Alyosha, in turn, kisses Ivan.

Dostoevsky said the next book, the life and teachings of the elder Zosima, was his answer to Ivan, given not as an argument but as a way of living: humility, forgiveness, and the belief that each person is responsible to all.

full.text: Love all God's creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God's light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things.
full.author: Dostoevsky
full.work: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, Chapter III

full.html: Dmitri is convicted, though the reader learns more than the jury; Ivan breaks down under the weight of his own ideas; Dmitri finds in suffering a new sense of hope. The novel ends with Alyosha speaking to a group of schoolboys at the stone where their friend Ilyusha wanted to be buried:

full.text: ... still let us remember how good it was once here, when we were all together, united by a good and kind feeling which made us, for the time we were loving that poor boy, better perhaps than we are.
full.author: Dostoevsky
full.work: The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, Chapter III

full.html: Dostoevsky gave his strongest arguments to the doubter, Ivan, and many readers, believers and not, think Ivan's case is never answered in argument. Others find the answer in the lives of Zosima, Alyosha and the boys. The novel does not settle the question; it shows what each answer means in a human life.
Taking any one character as Dostoevsky's mouthpiece. He let each voice speak at full strength, so that the novel is, as later critics put it, a chorus of independent voices.

deep.text: The Karamazovs in the great conversation

items: The Book of Job and Augustine asked why a good God allows suffering; Ivan presses the question harder than almost any other book.
Kierkegaard and Pascal, on this ladder, also spoke of faith as a choice of the whole person.
Nietzsche, Dostoevsky's contemporary, asked what happens to morality "beyond good and evil"; Ivan's "everything is lawful" is Dostoevsky's version of the question.
Freud, later on this ladder, wrote an essay on this novel.
Can a person be responsible for something they did not do, but wished or encouraged?
Is it possible to answer suffering with an argument, or only with love and action?
Why might people give up freedom for bread and certainty?
What does Alyosha mean when he says one good memory can save a person?

questions: Which brother are you most like? Which would you want as a friend?
Father Zosima taught that we are responsible for each other. What does that mean in a family?
Why might someone find it hard to believe, even if they want to?
Alyosha said a good memory from childhood can help someone all their life. Do you have one?
Why do you think the novel ends with children, not with the trial?
